summary: A 1978 Telnet option for SUPDUP-Output, used together with the SUPDUP protocol to carry its display output over Telnet. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: This lets the fancy screen output of one tool travel inside an ordinary chat connection.

questions: what is the telnet supdup-output option
how does supdup output work over telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a server on an ordinary Telnet connection use SUPDUP screen control on the user's display.

tldr.problem: Display-oriented programs on a server that is not display-oriented could not use SUPDUP screen support, because the SUPDUP protocol and its Telnet option hand all screen management to the server for the whole connection.
tldr.mechanism: The SUPDUP-OUTPUT option (code 22) sends the user's terminal parameters in one subnegotiation and the server's screen control codes in others, while Telnet stays in effect.
tldr.outcome: Occasional display programs can control the user's screen explicitly, and without any such blocks the connection is indistinguishable from normal Telnet.

today: RFC 749 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why SUPDUP-OUTPUT
sections.content:
The option gives access to the virtual display support of the SUPDUP protocol (RFC 734) inside a standard Telnet connection. This is not possible with the standard SUPDUP protocol or the Telnet SUPDUP option (RFC 736), because after negotiation everything follows RFC 734 and the server takes total responsibility for screen management.

With SUPDUP-OUTPUT, Telnet stays in effect, and IAC IP and other Telnet commands remain valid. A display program on the server can control the user host's screen explicitly.
sections.eli5: Normally the computer far away just sends lines of text. This lets a program there also say exactly where to draw things on your screen.

sections.title: Negotiation and Terminal Parameters
sections.content:
The option code is SUPDUP-OUTPUT 22. Only the server may initiate it, by sending IAC WILL SUPDUP-OUTPUT. The user Telnet answers IAC DO or IAC DON'T. If it agrees, it must immediately send a description of the user's terminal, the terminal parameters from RFC 734, as six-bit bytes, one per eight-bit Telnet byte.

The block is IAC SB SUPDUP-OUTPUT 1 byte1 ... byten IAC SE. The code 1 is a command code kept for future extensions. Because IAC WON'T SUPDUP-OUTPUT is highly optional, the user Telnet should be ready to resend the parameters each time it receives IAC WILL SUPDUP-OUTPUT.
sections.eli5: First your computer describes your screen to the server, like telling a painter how big your canvas is.

sections.title: Screen Control Blocks
sections.content:
The server sends IAC SB SUPDUP-OUTPUT 2 N TD1 ... TDn SCx SCy IAC SE. The TD bytes are the %TDCODEs and printing characters of SUPDUP output. N counts them, may be zero, and may not be greater than 254. SCx and SCy give the expected horizontal and vertical cursor position after the user host interprets the codes.

Restrictions: the %TDORS output reset code may not be sent, no multi-byte TDCODE sequence such as %TDMOV or %TDILP may be split across blocks, and no byte in a block will be 255. The option says nothing about input, which defaults to NVT input.
sections.eli5: Each message says which drawing moves to make and where the pen should end up afterwards.

sections.title: Defaults and Status
sections.content: The default is WON'T SUPDUP-OUTPUT and DON'T SUPDUP-OUTPUT, so the format may not be sent. The user Telnet must keep track of the cursor across normal NVT output and SUPDUP-OUTPUT blocks, and may assume the server manages both in an integrated way. The RFC lists RFC 734, RFC 736 and RFC 747 as references.
sections.eli5: Unless both agree, nothing special happens, and the user's side keeps track of where the cursor is.
